e.t: This word means “to set before,” describing the act of placing or presenting something in front of someone for consideration. It is an action word: what is set before others is brought into their view or attention. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, once in Acts and once in Galatians. Its exact force in either verse depends on what is being presented and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains bringing something forward before another person.

This word describes someone who is not acquainted with or unacquainted with something. It points to a lack of familiarity or experience rather than necessarily opposition or rejection. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Hebrews 5:13. Its basic sense is therefore simple: a person who has not become familiar with a matter. The surrounding verse is needed to show exactly what the person is unfamiliar with in that passage.

This Greek New Testament word means “fasting” or “going without food.” It describes abstaining from eating, whether deliberately or as a condition resulting from circumstances. As a noun, it names the experience or practice of not taking food rather than an action directed toward another person. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 27:21. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the absence of food for a period of time.

This word means “without,” expressing the absence of a person, thing, or accompanying circumstance. It describes something done or existing apart from what might otherwise be present. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, both in Luke, so its basic sense is narrow and consistent rather than broad or varied. The surrounding words determine exactly what is absent in each sentence, but the word itself contributes the idea of lacking or being separate from something. Its two recorded occurrences are Luke 22:6 and Luke 22:35.

Bethany is the name of a place mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It is not a general descriptive word or an action; it identifies a particular location. The name appears twelve times, in twelve verses, across Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. It is rendered consistently as “Bethany,” showing that its role is to preserve the place name rather than translate it into an ordinary English description. The exact significance of Bethany in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative.

e.t: This verb means “to farm,” describing the work of cultivating land so it can produce a crop. It refers to agricultural labor rather than to the land itself or the harvest. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 6:7. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains the active work of farming and tending cultivated ground.

This word refers to a written document, especially a passage of Scripture or the Scriptures as a recognized body of writings. It can describe an individual written passage or Scripture more broadly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 50 times, showing regular use for written biblical material rather than merely for writing in general. Its meaning remains centered on something written and read as Scripture within the surrounding context.

This word refers to a heifer, a young female cow. It is a specific animal term rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Hebrews 9:13. Its precise significance there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself retains this straightforward meaning: a heifer used as an animal in the discussion. The English rendering consistently gives the same meaning.

e.t: This Greek word means “to arouse” or “to get up.” It describes awakening or rising, whether someone is stirred from rest or gets up. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times across five verses, including passages in Mark, Luke, John, and 2 Peter. Its exact sense—whether someone arouses another or rises themselves—comes from the sentence and surrounding context, but its central idea is movement from stillness or sleep into awakened activity.

Dorcas is a personal name, rendered “Dorcas” in the Greek New Testament. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. This word occurs twice in this corpus, both times in Acts 9:36 and Acts 9:39. Its basic meaning is therefore the person’s name; what is said about Dorcas in either passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek New Testament word usually expresses movement or direction toward a person, place, or goal, often meaning “to,” “into,” or “toward.” It can also serve more broadly for a resulting purpose or relation, reflected in the glosses “as” and “for.” As a preposition, its exact English rendering depends on the words around it. It occurs 1,767 times in the Greek New Testament, so it is a common word used in many kinds of sentences.

e.t: This word means “to hang upon,” describing something suspended from or clinging to something else. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 19:48. The basic sense is straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is hanging upon what. Its single occurrence means the word has a focused use in this corpus rather than a broad range of repeated applications.

e.t: This word means “to fall off,” “to fall out,” or, in one rendering, “had fallen out.” It describes something or someone moving away from a former position, place, or condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs ten times, including descriptions of falling away from a location and statements about something failing to remain as it was. Its exact force depends on the sentence, but the central idea is departure, falling away, or separation from where something previously stood.

This word refers to braiding—the arranging or intertwining of hair into a braided style. It names the hairstyle or hair-arranging practice itself rather than expressing an action, command, or character quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Peter 3:3, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: braiding or arranging hair by intertwining it.

Eubulus is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, in 2 Timothy 4:21, and is rendered “Eubulus.” Because this word functions as a person’s name, its basic meaning is identification: it tells the reader who is being mentioned. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the verse’s full wording.

This word means “divinely instructed” or “taught by God.” It describes someone whose understanding or conduct has been formed through God’s instruction, emphasizing God as the source of that teaching. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Thessalonians 4:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: receiving instruction that comes from God rather than merely from human teachers.

Jannes is a personal name referring to an individual named in the Greek New Testament. It does not describe a general quality, action, or object; it identifies a person. The name appears once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:8. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name itself supports only this identification, not further conclusions about the person’s character, actions, or significance. Its English rendering is also “Jannes,” preserving the name rather than translating it into a descriptive meaning.

e.t: This word means “to desire” or “to love,” expressing strong personal affection or longing toward someone. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 2:8. Its basic sense describes an inward attachment that moves a person to care deeply for another. The exact emphasis in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to genuine desire and loving affection rather than a detached or merely formal concern.

This word means “to spy” or “to spy on”—to watch someone secretly in order to observe or investigate them. It describes an action rather than a person or object. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Galatians 2:4. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise force there cannot be described further, but the central idea remains secret observation or investigation.

e.t: This word means “to gain,” describing the act of obtaining something or benefiting from an action. It is a verb, so it expresses what someone gains rather than naming the gain itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 17 times across 16 verses, including uses rendered “gain” and “gained.” Its range includes gaining something of value, gaining another person, or obtaining a result. The surrounding verse determines what is gained and how the action should be understood.

This word means “credit”: the acknowledgment assigned to someone for what has been done. It points to the value or commendation connected with a person’s conduct, while its precise force depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Peter 2:20. The word’s basic sense is therefore credit, not a broad description of every kind of reward or benefit.

This word means “hair,” referring to hair itself. It is used in the Greek New Testament to name something a person has, rather than an action or abstract quality. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 11:15. The word’s broader force in that passage depends on its surrounding context, but its basic lexical meaning remains simple and direct: hair.

This word refers to a robber or rebel—someone who takes what is not theirs and may act in open defiance. Its central sense is a person involved in violent or lawless opposition, not merely someone who quietly takes something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 15 times, including descriptions of robbers and of people treated as such. The related meanings “rebel” and “robber” are both represented in its biblical usage, with the surrounding passage determining which aspect is emphasized.

This word refers to a scheme or deliberate scheming—an organized plan or method used to accomplish an aim. It presents planning as purposeful and potentially deceptive rather than as a simple, open action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ephesians. Its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains an intentional strategy or calculated way of acting.

This word means “recompense” or “reward”—something given in return for what a person has done or endured. It points to a received return, whether viewed as repayment or as a promised benefit. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Hebrews, where it is consistently rendered “reward.” Its central idea is the outcome granted in response to faithful action, effort, or costly commitment, while the surrounding verse determines the particular situation being discussed.

e.t: This word means “to host” or “to receive a guest.” It describes welcoming someone as a guest, especially the act of offering hospitality or receiving a person into one’s care or household. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, so it represents a recurring term for welcoming or lodging guests rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This word means “to despise” or “to make light of,” expressing an attitude that treats someone or something as unworthy of respect or serious attention. In Hebrews 12:5, it describes the danger of dismissing the Lord’s discipline rather than recognizing its significance. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, so its ordinary meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse supplies its particular force.

This word means “and not,” “neither,” or “nor.” It joins negative statements, people, or things, showing that one item is not included and that another is not included either. Depending on the sentence, it may connect two or more parts of a negative statement. It is a common word in the Greek New Testament, occurring 87 times, so its exact force is understood by the words and clauses it joins.

This word means “innkeeper,” a person responsible for receiving and caring for travelers at an inn. It is a noun describing the person who manages such lodging, rather than the building itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 10:35. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the person entrusted with an inn and its guests.

This word means “rudder,” the steering device used to guide a boat or ship. It is a concrete noun referring to equipment that helps direct a vessel’s movement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts 27:40 and James 3:4, both times referring to a ship’s rudder. The word itself names the instrument, while the surrounding passage determines what point is being made with it.

e.t: This word means “to lead astray”: to cause someone to move away from what is true, right, or reliable. It can describe misleading people through false teaching, mistaken claims, or deceptive influence. The word is used 39 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in 37 verses, so it describes a recurring danger rather than a rare idea. Its references include warnings about people being led astray and accounts of mistaken understanding. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the deceiver, the person misled, or the false belief itself.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to foretell” or “to predict”—to state beforehand what will happen. It refers to announcing something in advance rather than merely describing an event after it occurs. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, in Galatians 5:21 and 1 Thessalonians 4:6. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic idea remains speaking beforehand about a future matter.

This word means “perseverance”: continuing faithfully and refusing to give up. It describes steady persistence rather than a momentary effort, highlighting the resolve to remain committed over time. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 6:18. The word’s basic sense is therefore focused and clear, though the surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly how perseverance functions there. Its English rendering is consistently “perseverance,” reinforcing the idea of sustained steadfastness.

This word means “carriage,” referring to a vehicle used for transportation. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 18:13. The word identifies an item being counted among valuable goods, but the specific force of its use depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains straightforward: a carriage, something used to convey people or belongings from one place to another.

Sala is a personal name, used to identify an individual rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke 3. The English rendering preserves the name as “Sala,” so it is not normally translated into a broader descriptive meaning. Its precise significance in either occurrence belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a name.

This word refers to continuance or an uprising. It can describe something remaining or continuing, or a disturbance in which people rise up against established order. Its exact sense depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, including passages in Mark, Luke, Acts, and Hebrews, so its use spans both public unrest and statements about continuation. The central idea is either persistence or collective rising, with context showing which meaning is intended.

This word means “to distort”: to twist something away from its proper shape, meaning, or presentation. It describes an action that makes something crooked or misrepresented rather than clear and sound. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 3:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on altering something so that it no longer reflects it rightly.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, first, Singular

e.t: This word means “to rob”: to take something from another person unlawfully. It describes the act of seizing what does not belong to you, rather than simply receiving or borrowing it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 11:8. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular situation in which Paul used it, but the word itself points plainly to wrongful taking or plundering.

This word means “four months,” describing a period whose length is measured as four months. It refers to a span of time rather than to a person, place, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at John 4:35. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its direct meaning remains a simple time measurement: a period lasting four months.

This word means “beyond,” expressing something that lies farther than a stated point, limit, or boundary. It directs attention past what has already been reached or considered. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 10:16. Its basic sense is spatial or figurative extension beyond a recognized limit, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being exceeded. The word itself emphasizes moving or reaching farther than the present boundary.

This Greek New Testament word refers to a deep place, especially a well or an abyss. It describes an actual source or pit of depth in some passages, while in Revelation it refers to the abyss. The central idea is a deep hollow or opening in the earth. It occurs seven times in five New Testament verses, with the sense of “well” appearing in John and the sense of “abyss” appearing in Revelation. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means a “den,” “dens,” or “hole”—a hollow place that can serve as a dwelling or refuge. It is a concrete noun describing an animal’s shelter or hiding place, rather than an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 8:20 and Luke 9:58. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a den or hole.

This word refers to a psalm or to the book of Psalms. It names sacred songs and the collected Psalms in the Greek New Testament. The word appears seven times, including references to the Psalms as Scripture and instructions involving psalms in gathered worship. Its precise role in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains a psalm or the Psalms as a recognized body of sacred songs.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “like,” “as,” or “about,” expressing comparison or an approximate amount. It helps connect one thing with another by showing resemblance, or indicates that a number or age is not exact. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 21 times across 20 verses, including uses rendered “like” and “about.” Its precise force depends on the sentence: it may describe how something appears, how people are arranged, or an approximate figure.
